"I worked at the (Youngstown) Sheet & Tube Co. from 1974 until Black Monday," Sanders, of Vienna, said, referring to Sept. 19, 1977 -- the day the company's Campbell Works suddenly closed, idling more than 5,000 steelworkers and marking the start of the area steel industry's demise. During his three years with the company, Sanders, who also served the same amount of time in the U.S. Army from 1971 to 1974, worked as a laborer and a brakeman who also placed slag materials in the furnace. Sanders was among those who brought his recollections to the Mahoning Valley Heritage Association Museum's P&LE Day on Saturday morning at the museum on the Jim Marter Yard, 1340 Poland Ave., on the South Side. The three-hour gathering paid homage to the Pittsburgh & Lake Erie Railroad, also known as the "Little Giant," that was chartered in May 1875. The Pittsburgh-based rail company was pivotal in carrying massive quantities of iron ore, coke, limestone, coal and steel to the Mahoning Valley's burgeoning steel mills. "Today, we highlight the P&LE, one of the railroads that serviced the steel mills when they were running," Mike McCleery, the museum's treasurer and secretary, said. The rail also was a key part of the region's industrial history, added McCleery, who retired after having worked 33 years at General Motors Corp.'s Lordstown plant. The P&LE Railroad began operating in 1879 and started as a single-track railroad that connected Pittsburgh and Youngstown, and by 1890, it became among the main rail routes in the eastern U.S. The railroad continued to grow in the 20th century, thanks largely to advances in technology, according to www.historicpittsburgh.org. As all-steel cars developed, the trains were able to carry loads of up to 50 tons. In addition, advancements in brake technology allowed the trains to carry heavier loads of coal while running faster and safer, the website shows. The Marter Yard is to have about 15 train cars on its three sets of tracks. Two of them are in Struthers and two more are on the other side of the Mahoning River from the museum, McCleery said, adding that the yard formerly was a parking lot for Republic Steel. The museum, which he described as containing "a little bit of history up close and personal," is in a 76-year-old yellow caboose with a metal stove, ice box and lockers, as well as a space in the front for the conductor and a work area in the back. Among the memorabilia outside of the museum were an original radio that was used to communicate with different departments and the trains, painted lanterns that were on P&LE cars, a train schedule from Dec. 4, 1898, an original switch key, a manual detailing safety rules, time sheets and a photo album with numerous photographs of steelworkers, train cars and newspaper articles. Also included was a black-and-white photo snapped in 1961 of a blast furnace on Republic Steel's property close to the original Center Street Bridge in Campbell. Also during the event Saturday, Joe Vasko and Carl Jacobson, the museum's vice president and president, respectively, worked to reassemble an old three-panel switch stand that contains what were called "retarders" that slowed a train's wheels and allowed it to safely and gently roll down a hill to stop. Its other feature is an elaborate network of switches lining 35 sets of railroad tracks, the same number of tracks that led into and out of the Gateway Yard, which the P&LE operated on more than 200 acres near the original Center Street Bridge. The yard, built in 1957, sorted railcars.laden with raw materials and finished products for the steel industry. It closed in 1993, though portions of trackage are still used for short-line and freight operations. The yard, tower and other structures still stand, however, and are visible from Wilson Avenue. The switch stand will eventually be part of the museum's permanent display, but for now, it will be temporarily housed in a secure, water-tight storage building, Vasko said. The nonprofit Mahoning Valley Railroad Heritage Association was established in 1985 to preserve railroading history in the Mahoning Valley, with an emphasis on the steel industry. In the MVRHA's early days, the organization began to collect railroad equipment, and in 2007, it acquired 3.5 acres from the city for its current location. For more information about the MVRHA, go to www.mvrha.org. Starting at /week. Subscribe Today

https://www.dw.com/en/germany-sets-its-s.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MMQl Royal Marine Commandos detained a sanctioned tanker, the Smyrtos, in the English Channel in June 2026 Image: LPhot Hutchins/Royal Navy/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement On September 1, when the German government publicly blamed Russia for the failed drone attack on Leipzig Airport, it announced a series of retaliatory measures. Among them was a tougher crackdown on the so-called Russian shadow fleet. The term refers to often aging, poorly maintained and inadequately insured vessels, mostly oil tankers, with opaque ownership structures, which Russia uses in an attempt to circumvent sanctions . But detaining such vessels is far from straightforward, Julian Pawlak, a maritime security expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, told DW. International maritime law, he noted, is fundamentally designed to protect the freedom of commercial shipping. "The transport of these goods on the high seas is not, in itself, illegal," Pawlak explains. "What complicates matters is that parts of this shadow fleet are linked to so-called hybrid activities , including acts of sabotage, espionage, and possibly drone operations and related disruptions." Germany has not done enough to address the issue so far, argues Sara Nanni, a security policy spokesperson for the Green Party . In a recent interview with DW, she complained: "Russia is financing both its war against Ukraine and its aggressive behavior toward Europe through its shadow fleet." Action must be taken against it, she said. "That is the only thing that could persuade Russia to return to the negotiating table." Germany blames Russia for attempted terror attack in Leipzig To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video She accuses the German government of failing to take action: "Other countries are doing it in the Baltic Sea , but Germany isn't. I keep hearing the interior minister say that it is technically or legally difficult. But I believe the decision not to do it is a political one. And I think it is wrong." Finland shows another way to tackle the shadow fleet By "other countries," she is referring, for example, to Finland. In late 2024, the tanker "Eagle S" damaged the Estlink 2 power cable in the Gulf of Finland by dragging an anchor across the seabed. Finnish border guards subsequently detained the vessel. Although a court later dismissed charges of aggravated criminal damage, Sönke Marahrens, a security expert at Kiel University, praised the Finnish response in an interview with DW: "They sent a clear message to the other side: We know what you're doing, and we're stopping you. And you could see that after this clear warning, the other side got the message and changed its behavior." In addition to Finland, the United Kingdom, France and Sweden have also adopted a tougher approach toward suspicious vessels. Within its territorial waters, the Swedish Coast Guard specifically targets tankers and cargo ships suspected of belonging to the shadow fleet for inspection. Vessels are routinely detained if they are found to be carrying forged documents, lack adequate insurance, pose a risk to maritime safety or violate environmental regulations. Russia's threats: just a bluff? It is easy to assume that the German government's restraint is aimed at avoiding an escalation with Russia. That impression is reinforced by the fact that the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which is considered right-wing extremist in parts, won the state election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on a platform that, despite the war in Ukraine, advocates closer relations between Germany and Russia. According to opinion polls, concerns about the prospect of war in Europe were also a decisive factor for many voters. Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, even described Germany's accusations against Moscow as "the beginning of a real war." Johannes Peters of the Institute for Security Policy at Kiel University, however, believes such fears are unfounded. "Other European countries have taken a more robust approach, and despite those concerns, and indeed despite Russian rhetoric, very little has actually happened," Peters said. "Russia has not escalated the situation. Instead, it has largely steered clear of confrontation. In particular, we have seen that laden tankers, which are extremely valuable, are now avoiding Swedish waters because Sweden has stepped up efforts to stop and inspect vessels." After the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said: "The federal government will make those responsible for hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for it." Peters believes: "If you use strong rhetoric, sooner or later you have to back it up with action. The chancellor has put the government under pressure to follow through." Why did Norway seize a Russian ship for Ukraine? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Armed Russian crews on board Security expert Pawlak, however, cautions that inspecting suspicious Russian vessels is not without risk. "Of course, any such operation has to take into account the possibility that Russian warships may be escorting these vessels or, as has increasingly been the case, that armed crews with ties to Russian mercenary groups may be on board," Pawlak said. "Those are risks that must be factored into the equation." Estonia experienced those risks firsthand in the case of the oil tanker "Jaguar." In May 2025, the vessel's captain ignored instructions from the Estonian authorities while passing through the country's coastal waters. Estonian officials attempted to stop and inspect the suspicious tanker. Russia responded by scrambling a fighter jet, prompting Estonia to stand down and allow the vessel to continue on its way. "It is important to consider the region in which these activities are taking place," Pawlak says. "In the Baltic Sea, Russia is naturally much closer geographically and therefore has other options at its disposal, including the deployment of military units in support." Farther afield, however, for example in the English Channel between the United Kingdom and France, that becomes more difficult: "Russia cannot escort or protect every shadow fleet vessel." Explained: How Germany will expand intel powers, and why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Inspections would raise costs for Russia While maritime security specialist Johannes Peters firmly supports taking action against shadow-fleet vessels where justified, he cautions against harboring illusions. "We are not going to be able to shut down this shadow-fleet system through inspections alone," he said. "Rather, the aim is to saddle Russia's shadow fleet with risks and uncertainties and to increase the costs of operating it." He offers a simple example: "If only one ship a day can make the journey instead of three, that translates into losses of hundreds of millions of euros a day. If a voyage takes not x days but x plus four, that, too, cuts into Russia's earnings. And revenue from oil exports is vital to Russia's war economy." This article has been translated from German. What Germany's move to officially blame Russia for the suspected hybrid attack at Leipzig airport means for Germany and NATO was the topic of discussion in DW's weekly Berlin Briefing podcast. Photograph: Indonesian Navy/EPA View image in fullscreen The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony. Photograph: Indonesian Navy/EPA Indonesia Indonesia gets its first aircraft carrier amid debate over cost and military ambitions The gift from Italy has sparked fierce debate among defence analysts and opposition politicians who question its true cost and purpose Associated Press Fri 18 Sep 2026 00.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Indonesia has received its first aircraft carrier, a former Italian warship that the government says will strengthen the archipelagic nation’s maritime security and disaster response capabilities. The 41-year-old former ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi, with capacity for short takeoff and vertical landing aircraft and helicopters, arrived Friday morning at a naval base in North Jakarta’s Tanjung Priok port, where it was welcomed with a military ceremony. Italy in March agreed to give the carrier, which was retired in 2024, to Indonesia in a move aimed at boosting Italy’s broader defence engagement with the south-east Asian country. Italy is seeking deals on submarines and aircraft, and gifting the carrier to Indonesia also saves it the cost of decommissioning the ship. View image in fullscreen Indonesia’s first aircraft carrier, the ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi (C), arrives at Tanjung Priok port in Jakarta. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA The transfer would make Indonesia only the second country in south-east Asia with a carrier in its fleet. The first was Thailand’s HTMS Chakri Naruebet, which was commissioned in 1997 after being procured from Spain along with carrier-capable AV-8S Matador jump-jets. The carrier will be formally commissioned into the Indonesian Navy next week as the KRI Gajah Mada, named after the famed 14th-century Majapahit-era military leader, whose campaigns and vision of a unified archipelago have made him one of Indonesia’s most celebrated historical figures. The women saving Borneo: battling fire, patriarchy and super El Niño on Indonesia’s peatland frontlines Read more Defence development was one of the top priorities for president Prabowo Subianto’s administration, as he has advocated an expansion of the military through the purchase of submarines, frigates, fighter jets, missiles and pushed for more defence cooperation with various countries. But the Garibaldi acquisition has sparked a fierce debate among defence analysts, economists and opposition politicians who question whether Indonesia needs an aircraft carrier at all and whether the government should be spending millions of dollars to refurbish and operate an ageing warship while facing mounting fiscal pressures at home. Indonesia’s finance ministry approved $450m in financing for the aircraft carrier program in 2025. However, some lawmakers have warned the overall bill could be far higher. TB Hasanuddin, a member of parliament’s Commission I, said the cost of retrofitting the carrier alone could reach 16tn rupiah (about $900m). View image in fullscreen The aircraft carrier ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi sailing near Bangka Belitung island. Photograph: Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet Command Public Relations Office/AFP/Getty Images Unlike major naval powers that use aircraft carriers to launch fighter jets far from home shores, Indonesia views the vessel as a mobile command centre and support hub for helicopters, drones and maritime operations across its thousands of islands. Speaking during a disaster management meeting early this month, Prabowo said the vessel would help authorities combat forest and peatland fires that regularly blanket parts of south-east Asia with hazardous haze. Prabowo said the carrier could accommodate up to 10 medium-sized helicopters, including aircraft with capabilities comparable to the Black Hawk and Mi-17, and could carry large quantities of water and be deployed to areas with large numbers of fire hotspots. He also outlined plans to operate drones from the ship and use it as a mobile platform that could be rapidly deployed to help in the event of natural disasters, which are common in Indonesia, a nation that sits in the Pacific “Ring of Fire.” View image in fullscreen The through-deck aviation cruiser class ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi docks in Indonesia. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA Operating a carrier is extremely costly, however, and experts have questioned whether Indonesia’s leadership has thought through whether one is necessary for the country’s defence or disaster-relief needs. The acquisition comes as Indonesia’s economy faces growing fiscal pressures. Prabowo’s government has been funding a free nutritious meals program – which has been tainted by multiple food poisoning incidents – and other costly initiatives while economists have warned about slowing growth, weaker state revenues and widening budget constraints, prompting closer scrutiny of major government spending projects. View image in fullscreen Experts have warned that operating a carrier is extremely costly. Photograph: Indonesian Navy 2nd Fleet Command Public Relations Office/AFP/Getty Images “The plan to acquire the Garibaldi must be based on genuine operational needs and our ability to operate it, rather than being driven by pride or other considerations,” said Muhammad Fauzan Malufti, of the Center for Strategic and International Studies. El Niño-fuelled wildfires destroy precious Indonesian forests – in pictures Read more He said policymakers must weigh not only the vessel’s acquisition and modernisation costs, but also the Navy’s ability to sustain its operations, including personnel, maintenance, fuel, weapons systems and supporting infrastructure. Fauzan said the government should be transparent about those considerations, particularly given the vessel’s age. He cited Thailand’s carrier as a cautionary example, saying it has spent much of its service life in port because of operational and budget constraints. “The bottom line is that this should not be forced. Otherwise, the benefits could be outweighed by the costs,” Fauzan said. “The money might be better spent on other priorities, such as increasing the number of frigates in the fleet.” View image in fullscreen Indonesian defence minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin on the ITS Giuseppe Garibaldi. Photograph: Mast Irham/EPA Military analyst Khairul Fahmi of the Institute for Security and Strategic Studies said aircraft carriers are not a priority for Indonesia, which is focused on preventing adversaries from operating freely in the country’s territorial waters. “Indonesia has a greater need for submarines, frigates and asymmetric weapons systems to protect its maritime sovereignty,” he said. But he added that if Indonesia is seeking to position itself as a major maritime nation, “an aircraft carrier can be both a symbol of national power and a multifunctional platform capable of supporting a wide range of military and non-military missions.” Explore more on these topics Indonesia Asia Pacific Prabowo Subianto news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development
